reference.title: Branch, Tag, History, and Blame Actions

section.title: Show Staging
section.p: Use: Opens the Git Staging view.

Details: The Git Staging view is the main place where you review working copy changes, compare files, stage changes, write commit messages, commit, push, and pull. Opening the view does not change the repository.
Accessible From: Git menu.

section.title: Show Branches or Show Git Branch Manager View
section.p: Use: Opens the Git Branch Manager view.

Details: The branch manager shows local branches and remote branches for the current repository. Branches are named lines of development. Use this view to inspect branch state, checkout branches, create branches, merge branches, and configure remote branch tracking.

section.title: Checkout
section.p: Use: Switches the local repository to the selected branch, remote branch, tag, or commit, depending on the context.

Details: Checkout changes which revision is active in the working copy. When you checkout a local branch, the working copy is updated to that branch. When you checkout a remote branch, Git creates a local branch from it. Checking out a tag or commit lets you view the repository at that point in history.
Scope: Selected branch, remote branch, tag, or commit.

ul.li: Contextual menu in the Git Branch Manager view local branch actions.
Contextual menu in the Git History view history table.

section.title: Create Branch
section.p: Use: Creates a branch from the selected branch or commit.

Details: A branch is a movable name that points to a commit. Creating a branch lets you start a separate line of work from an existing branch or from a specific commit in history. By default, the new branch is checked out after it is created.
Best Practice: Deselect Checkout branch in the Create branch dialog box if you only want to create the branch and keep working on the current branch.

ul.li: Contextual menu in the Git Branch Manager view.
Contextual menu in the Git History view.

section.title: Track Remote Branch
section.p: Use: Lets you select the remote branch that the local branch tracks for fetch, push, and pull commands.

Details: A tracking branch defines the relationship between a local branch and a remote branch. The Git Client uses this relationship to know where to pull from and where to push commits. Use this action when a local branch should synchronize with a different remote branch.
Scope: Selected local branch or current local branch.

ul.li: Local branch contextual menu in the Git Branch Manager view.

section.title: Merge Selected Branch or Commit
section.p: Use: Merges the selected branch or commit into the current branch.

Details: Merge integrates changes that are reachable from the selected branch or commit but not already in the current branch. If the histories diverged, Git may create a merge commit. If the same files changed in incompatible ways, conflicts must be resolved before the merge can finish.
Scope: Selected branch or commit and current branch.

ul.li: Local branch contextual menu in the Git Branch Manager view.
Commit contextual menu in the Git History view.

section.title: Rebase...
section.p: Use: Rebases the current branch's local commits onto the selected commit.

Details: Rebase replays the commits from the current branch on top of the selected commit, producing a linear history. A confirmation dialog box shows the name of the current branch before the operation starts. If the rebase completes cleanly, the Git History view and the Git Staging view refresh automatically. If conflicts occur, a warning dialog box lists the conflicting files and the repository enters a rebase-in-progress state. Resolve the conflicts in the Git Staging view, then use Continue Rebase to finish or Abort Rebase to cancel. If the repository already has unresolved conflicts when the action is triggered, an error message is shown and the rebase does not start. If uncommitted changes would be overwritten, a warning dialog box lists the affected files.
Scope: Current branch and selected commit.

Best Practice: Because rebase rewrites local commit history, use it only for commits that have not been pushed to a shared remote branch. After rebasing, a force push is required to update the remote branch.
Accessible From: Commit contextual menu in the Git History view history table. Not available on the Uncommitted changes row.

section.title: Squash Merge Selected Branch
section.p: Use: Merges changes from the selected branch since it diverged from the current branch and records the result in a new commit on the current branch.

Details: A squash merge applies the combined file changes from another branch without preserving each individual commit from that branch. The current branch receives one new commit that contains the final result.
Scope: Selected branch and current branch.
Accessible From: Local branch contextual menu in the Git Branch Manager view.

section.title: Show in History
section.p: Use: Selects the commit that corresponds to the HEAD of the selected branch in the Git History view.
Details: HEAD identifies the current tip of a branch. Use this action to jump from a branch in the branch manager to the matching commit in history and inspect the commit details or affected files.
Scope: Selected branch.
Accessible From: Local branch contextual menu in the Git Branch Manager view.

section.title: Delete Branch
section.p: Use: Deletes the selected local branch.

Details: Deleting a branch removes the local branch name from the repository. It does not delete commits that are still reachable from another branch or tag. You must switch to another branch before you can delete the current branch.
Caution: Before deleting a branch, make sure its work was merged, pushed, or is no longer needed.
Accessible From: Local branch contextual menu in the Git Branch Manager view.

section.title: Show Tags
section.p: Use: Opens a dialog box that lists all tags in the current repository.

Details: A tag is a name assigned to a specific commit, often used for releases or stable milestones. From the tag list, you can delete tags, checkout a specific tag, or push a local-only tag to the remote repository.

section.title: Create Tag
section.p: Use: Creates a tag on the selected commit.
Details: Creating a tag assigns a stable name to a commit. Tags are useful for marking releases or other important points in history. A new tag is local until you push it to the remote repository.
Scope: Selected commit.
Accessible From: Commit contextual menu in the Git History view.

section.title: Show History or Show Current Repository History
section.p: Use: Opens the Git History view for the current repository, selected resource, or current file.

Details: History shows commits, authors, dates, messages, and affected resources. Use it to inspect how the repository or a specific file changed over time, compare versions, open previous versions, create tags, cherry-pick commits, or revert commits.
Scope: Current repository, selected resource, or current file.

ul.li: Contextual Git submenus in supported views and editors.

section.title: Cherry-Pick
section.p: Use: Applies the changes from the selected commit to the current branch.

Details: Cherry-pick copies the change introduced by one commit and creates a new commit with that change on the current branch. It is useful when you need one fix or feature from another branch without merging the entire branch.
Scope: Selected commit and current branch.
Accessible From: Commit contextual menu in the Git History view.

section.title: Revert Commit
section.p: Use: Creates a commit that reverses all changes from the selected commit.
Details: Revert does not remove the original commit from history. Instead, it adds a new commit with the opposite changes. This makes it safe for commits that were already shared with other users.
Best Practice: Use revert instead of reset when you need to undo a commit that was already shared.
Accessible From: Commit contextual menu in the Git History view.

section.title: Reset Branch to Commit
section.p: Use: Moves the HEAD of the current branch to the selected commit.

Details: Reset changes which commit the current branch points to. Depending on the reset mode used by the workflow, it can also affect the index or working copy. Because it can rewrite branch history, it can cause problems if the branch was already shared.
Caution: Reset can change branch history. Use it with care, especially on branches shared with other users.
Accessible From: Commit contextual menu in the Git History view.

section.title: Explain Commit
section.p: Use: Uses AI Positron to explain the changes from the selected commits.
Details: The action analyzes the selected commits and generates an explanation of the changes.
Scope: Selected commits.
Accessible From: Commit contextual menu in the Git History view.

section.title: Open Previous Version
section.p: Use: Opens the version of the selected resource from before its deletion.
Details: When a file was deleted in a commit, this action opens the last version that existed before the deletion. Use it to inspect removed content without restoring the file to the working copy.
Availability: Available for deleted resources.
Accessible From: Affected resources pane in the Git History view.

section.title: Open Working Copy Version
section.p: Use: Opens the working copy version of the selected resource.

Details: The working copy version is the file as it currently exists on disk. Use this action to compare a historical resource entry with the file you are currently editing. It also works if the resource was renamed between versions.
Availability: Available for added and modified resources.
Accessible From: Affected resources pane in the Git History view.

section.title: Reset File to This Commit
section.p: Use: Performs a checkout of the selected version of the resource and overwrites its current working copy version.

Details: This action restores one file to the content it had in the selected commit. It affects the file in the working copy, not the entire branch. It does not work if the resource was renamed or deleted between versions.
Caution: This action overwrites the current working copy version of the selected file.
Accessible From: Affected resources pane in the Git History view.

section.title: Compare with Previous Version
section.p: Use: Compares the selected version of the resource with the previous version.
Details: This action shows what changed in the selected resource at that point in history. Use it to review the difference introduced by a commit for one modified file.
Availability: Available for modified resources.
Accessible From: Affected resources pane in the Git History view.

section.title: Compare with Working Copy Version
section.p: Use: Compares the selected version of the resource with the current working copy version.

Details: Use this action to see how the current file differs from a version recorded in repository history. It helps when you need to understand whether current local work already includes, changes, or removes older content.
Availability: Available for modified resources.
Accessible From: Affected resources pane in the Git History view.

section.title: Compare with Each Other
section.p: Use: Compares two selected versions of a single file with each other.
Details: This action shows how a file changed between two selected points in history. Use it when the current working copy is not the version you need to compare against.
Availability: Available when selecting two versions of a single file.
Accessible From: Affected resources pane in the Git History view.

section.title: Show Blame
section.p: Use: Opens the selected resource in the main editing area and colors editor lines based on revision information.

Details: Git blame associates each line with the commit that last changed it. Use it to find when a line changed, who changed it, and which commit introduced the change. When you select a line in the editor, the corresponding entry is highlighted in the history table in the Git History view.
Scope: Selected resource or current editor file.
